title: Login hours, IP ranges, session settings, MFA, and connected apps
objectives: Separate profile login hours and login IP ranges from org-wide trusted IP ranges that only skip identity verification.
Place MFA on the authentication path and session settings on the authenticated connection, not as permission grants.
Explain that connected apps have their own OAuth and IP policies that can differ from browser login.
Diagnose a blocked login versus a timed-out session versus a connected-app token restricted by IP.
diagnostic_question: LAB_Agent cannot log in from home after 18:00, LAB_Rep is prompted for a verification code at a café Wi-Fi, LAB_Integration's connected app fails from a new data center IP, and a manager wants to 'raise session timeout to give them admin.' Which control is each, and which is not a permission set?
definition: Login hours on a profile limit when those users may log in. Profile login IP ranges can block login from addresses outside the range. Org trusted IP ranges (Network Access) do not by themselves block login; they skip extra identity verification from known networks. After login, session settings control timeout and session security. MFA requires additional verification methods at login. Connected apps apply OAuth access policies, including IP relaxation, that may differ from interactive login. ([Session Security](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_overview_sessions.htm); [What Is MFA?](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.basics_identity_mfa.htm))
why_it_matters: These controls look like 'access' but they are mostly when/where/how you authenticate and keep a session, not which objects you can use. Mixing them with permission sets or sharing wastes time. Connected apps are a common production miss: browser login works, the integration still fails on IP policy.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a shift-work loading dock. The posted shift board is login hours: after closing you do not start a new shift. The staff-only gate with a hard turnstile is profile IP ranges: wrong street, no entry. The sticker on the office Wi-Fi that skips a second ID check is org trusted IPs. The time clock that auto-clocks you out after idle time is session timeout. The second ID at the door is MFA. The vendor truck's own gate pass is the connected app—it is not the employee turnstile.
deeper_explanation: Trailhead's org-access module, pointing at Salesforce Help, distinguishes org trusted IP ranges from profile login IP ranges: trusted org ranges bypass verification codes for known networks, while users can still log in from elsewhere after verifying identity. Profile login IP ranges, when used, mean users outside the range cannot log in. Reverify the live Help articles Restrict Login IP Ranges and Network Access in the target org. ([Control Login Access](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_restricting_logins.htm); [Network Access](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_networkaccess.htm))

Login hours are specified per profile. Help-oriented training states that if users are logged in when hours end, they can continue to view the current page but cannot take further action. Confirm the wording on the profile Login Hours page in the org rather than inventing extra lockout timers.

Session Security Help: after login a session is established. Default inactivity timeout is two hours unless Session Settings change. Session security levels (Standard vs High Assurance) can gate sensitive operations. Timeout is not a permission grant. ([Session Security](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_overview_sessions.htm))

Salesforce requires MFA for user-interface logins. MFA asks for a second factor after username and password. It does not assign permission sets. ([What Is MFA?](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.basics_identity_mfa.htm))

Connected-app OAuth policies include IP relaxation: whether tokens are restricted to trusted IP ranges. Browser success does not prove the connected app will accept a new data-center IP. ([Connected App IP policies](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.shr_manage_oauth_access_policies_for_a_connected_app_ip_relaxation.htm))

mental_model.analogy: A shift-work loading dock: shift board = login hours, hard turnstile = profile IP ranges, office-Wi-Fi sticker = org trusted IPs, idle time clock = session, second ID = MFA, vendor gate pass = connected app.
useful_mapping: hard turnstile → profile login IP ranges (block)
Wi-Fi sticker skipping second check → org Network Access trusted IPs
vendor gate pass → connected app OAuth/IP policy
where_it_breaks: SSO identity providers may perform MFA before Salesforce sees the user (SEC-001).
High-assurance session policies can feel like authorization but remain session security.
Connected apps also have permission and scope models; this lesson only introduces IP/session adjacency.

teach_back_prompt: Explain why a café verification prompt is not the same as a profile IP block, and why a connected app can fail when Lightning still works.

review_schedule.prompt: Org trusted IP vs profile login IP vs login hours vs session timeout vs MFA vs connected app.

Two-minute interview: these are not permission sets.

claims.claim: After login a session is established. The documented default inactivity timeout is two hours. Session security levels can require High Assurance for sensitive operations.
MFA requires multiple factors at login and is required for Salesforce UI logins. It is not a permission grant.
Connected-app IP relaxation can restrict OAuth access tokens to trusted IP ranges, independent of a successful browser session.

Login hours and login IP restrictions are login-path controls documented under restricting login access; org Network Access ranges are a distinct trusted-network control. Reverify profile-block versus verification-skip behavior on the live Help pages.
claims.validation: Restrict Login Access and Network Access Help.

changed_in_release: MFA remains required for UI logins. Reverify Session Settings and connected-app IP policies in the target org.
unresolved_uncertainty: Exact profile Login Hours end-of-shift behavior should be confirmed on the live profile page Help.
Connected-app token lifetimes and refresh-token policies are neighboring OAuth topics; do not invent numbers.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Login hours and profile IPs decide when and where login is allowed. Org trusted IPs mainly skip extra verification. MFA is a second factor. Session settings govern the connection after login. Connected apps have their own IP/OAuth policies. None of these is a permission set.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I split tickets. Never logged in: hours, profile IP, MFA, IdP. Verification prompt at a café: probably not in org trusted IPs. Idle logout: session timeout, default two hours unless changed. Integration-only failure: connected app IP relaxation. Missing Setup: go back to user permissions. I will not raise timeout to grant admin.

terminology.confusable_neighbor: Session timeout: idle after login, not the shift board.
terminology.boundary: Configured on the profile, not on a permission set overlay in this lesson.

terminology.plain: Addresses from which that profile may log in.

terminology.non_example: Org Network Access trusted IPs that only skip a verification challenge.

terminology.plain: Org-known networks that skip extra identity verification.
terminology.precise: Network Access ranges. Users outside can still log in after verifying identity, unless a profile IP block also applies.
terminology.example: Office range added so campus Wi-Fi does not prompt a code every time.
terminology.boundary: Confirm live Network Access Help wording.

terminology.plain: How long and how strictly the authenticated connection lasts.
terminology.precise: Timeout, locking, security levels. Default inactivity timeout two hours.
terminology.example: Idle LAB_Rep sees the continue-or-logout prompt.
terminology.non_example: Granting View Setup by lengthening timeout.

terminology.plain: A second proof of identity at login.
terminology.precise: Multiple factors from different categories. Required for Salesforce UI logins.
terminology.boundary: SSO MFA may run at the IdP (SEC-001).

terminology.plain: An application that connects to Salesforce with OAuth (or SAML) policies of its own.

interview_questions.question: How do login hours, IP ranges, session settings, MFA, and connected apps differ?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Hours and profile IPs gate when/where login may occur. Org trusted IPs skip extra verification. MFA is a second factor. Session settings govern the connection after login. Connected apps have separate OAuth/IP policies. None is a permission set.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use a timeline. Before session: hours, profile IP, MFA, maybe IdP. During session: timeout and High Assurance. Beside the browser: connected-app tokens. I distinguish org Network Access from profile Login IP Ranges because one is often a skip and the other can be a wall. I refuse to mix in OWD.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Agent hours, LAB_Rep café code, LAB_ETL IP relaxation, refused timeout-as-admin.

interview_questions.question: Org trusted IPs versus profile login IP ranges?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Org Network Access trusted IPs skip extra identity verification on known networks; users can still log in from elsewhere after verifying. Profile login IP ranges, when used, can prevent login from outside the range.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I always re-read Restrict Login Access and Network Access rather than reciting a blog. The interview point is: a café verification prompt usually means you were allowed to continue after proving identity, so it was not a profile hard-block. A call-center profile that cannot log in from home is the hard-block pattern. I would not apply the hard-block to the only admin.
interview_questions.example: Office range in Network Access; LAB_CallCenter profile Login IP Ranges limited to that CIDR in a lab with a spare admin.
tradeoffs: Roaming users vs strict network control
weak_answer_warnings: Treating them as the same list

interview_questions.question: Call-center agents must not log in from home after shift. Design?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Profile login hours for the shift, and consider profile login IP ranges for the site. Do not use sharing or FLS as a clock. Keep a spare admin profile without those locks.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Situation: shift workers. Task: when/where login. Action: LAB_Agent profile hours in the correct time zone, optional IP allowlist, test Login History as LAB_Agent, not as System Administrator. I mention end-of-hours behavior should be confirmed on Help: they may still see the current page. Result: after-hours login fails without touching Opportunity CRUD.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Agent 09:00–18:00, office IP range, spare LAB_Admin unrestricted.
tradeoffs: Hours vs session timeout after they already logged in
follow_ups: What if they must finish a call after 18:00?

interview_questions.question: ETL fails from a new cloud IP; users are fine. Walk the diagnosis.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check the connected app's IP relaxation and OAuth policies, the integration user's login history, and whether Network Access or profile IP applies to that user. I do not open OWD.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Situation: UI green, job red. Task: find the token path. Action: connected app policies first, then the user the app impersonates, then org trusted ranges if the policy enforces them. I coordinate a documented IP add in a change window. Result: Lightning never needed a sharing change. I will not invent token TTLs.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ETL connected app Enforce IP Restrictions; new NAT not in range.
tradeoffs: IP allowlists vs compensating controls listed in Help
follow_ups: Does MFA apply to the integration user?

interview_questions.question: Users say Salesforce logs them out and they want System Administrator. Diagnose.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: If they were in and got an inactivity prompt, it is session timeout, default two hours unless changed. System Administrator is unrelated authorization. If they never got in, inspect hours, IP, MFA.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I reproduce. Session Management and Login History split 'never in' versus 'was in.' I read Session Settings. I keep MFA. I explain High Assurance if they were blocked from a sensitive Setup area rather than logged out. I will not lengthen timeout as a privilege grant. If they cannot see a record, I leave this topic.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep idle past org timeout; cloning System Administrator would not stop the prompt and would over-authorize.
tradeoffs: Security of short timeouts vs friction
follow_ups: Where do you see active sessions?
What is lock sessions to IP?

interview_questions.question: How does MFA fit next to login hours and IP ranges?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Hours and IPs decide if a login may be attempted from that time and place. MFA still proves identity when a login is allowed. You do not disable MFA because hours are tight.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: They stack. A user in hours and on a allowed IP still completes MFA for UI login. SSO may satisfy MFA at the IdP. Profile IP hard-blocks never reach MFA. Org trusted IPs may skip some verification codes but Salesforce still requires MFA for UI—do not confuse a network verification code with MFA itself. I keep least privilege on permissions separately.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Agent on campus during hours: MFA plus no café-style extra network code if the campus is trusted.

interview_questions.question: User gets a verification code at a hotel. Teammate wants to add the hotel IP to the profile Login IP Ranges. Risk?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: If you meant org trusted IPs, you are skipping extra verification for that network. If you instead set profile Login IP Ranges to only the hotel, you may hard-block the office. I would not add random hotel IPs without a policy.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate skip versus allowlist. Hotel IPs are ephemeral NAT. Putting them on a profile allowlist is operationally fragile and can lock the user out when the hotel changes. Better: complete the verification/MFA, use VPN onto a trusted range if policy allows, and keep profile hard-blocks for true site-only populations. I document the difference in the ticket so nobody 'fixes' Network Access by emptying Login IP Ranges.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep at a hotel completes a verification code; LAB_CallCenter profile remains office-only.
tradeoffs: Trusted range sprawl vs MFA prompts
weak_answer_warnings: Pasting hotel CIDR onto System Administrator

interview_questions.question: Teach the loading-dock analogy, then break it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Shift board is hours, turnstile is profile IP, Wi-Fi sticker is trusted org IPs, time clock is session, second ID is MFA, vendor pass is the connected app. It breaks for SSO MFA at an IdP and for High Assurance gating Setup.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk LAB_Agent off shift, LAB_Rep at a café, LAB_ETL at a new dock. I refuse timeout-as-admin. I then break the dock: SAML may authenticate elsewhere, High Assurance is a session level, OAuth scopes are more than a gate pass. Close: these controls are when/where/how, not CRUD or OWD.

tradeoffs: Memorable ops story vs Help precision
follow_ups: Where does SEC-001 stop and this start?
weak_answer_warnings: Calling connected apps a sharing rule
